item.title: Can Awe Actually Improve Mental Health?
item.description:
Awe

Can Awe Actually Improve Mental Health?

The first randomized controlled trial of awe reveals promising results.

Posted June 17, 2026

Key points
  • Researchers recently conducted the first randomized controlled trial focused on awe and mental health.
  • Results showed that participants practicing awe reported greater well-being and lower distress.
  • The findings hint at why nature, art, and spiritual practices can support mental health.
  • Awe doesn't always require the extraordinary — paying attention during ordinary life may be enough.

During the past two decades, a new science of awe emerged. Based on this research, some interpret awe as a powerful aid for many facets of human flourishing.

But it wasn't until recently that researchers used a randomized controlled trial (RCT) – the same study design often used to evaluate new medical treatments – to investigate whether awe can improve mental health. Because participants meeting specific criteria are randomly assigned to different conditions, RCTs provide stronger evidence about what helps most.

In this 2025 study, researchers worked with individuals living with long COVID, a population at increased risk for mental health struggles. Participants were randomly assigned either to begin an awe intervention immediately or to wait four weeks before starting. Everyone consented to this arrangement, and everyone eventually received the intervention.

For four weeks, participants learned a simple three-step process – one they were encouraged to practice at least three times each day. The researchers summarized the approach using the acronym AWE:

  1. Attention – giving full and undivided attention to things you appreciate, value, or find amazing.
  2. Waiting – slowing down and pausing.
  3. Exhaling and expanding – intentionally amplifying the sensations being experienced.

What I find fascinating about this intervention is how the researchers guided participants to experience awe. The instructions don’t emphasize something extraordinary like visiting the Grand Canyon, taking in the Northern Lights, or getting tickets to the World Cup. Rather, they suggest a daily practice that almost any of us could do. Basically, pay attention to what we find amazing, really take that in, and savor the experience.

So what happened?

Compared with those waiting to begin the intervention, participants who completed the awe program reported increases in awe and overall well-being, along with decreases in stress and depressive symptoms. From the beginning of the study to the end, those in the awe condition showed a 16% increase in well-being, a 12% decrease in stress, and a 17% decrease in depressive symptoms.

As someone who spends a good deal of time reading research, I'm still trying to figure out exactly what to make of these findings.

This is only one study, and I’m honestly not sure how “big” an effect is being revealed. A 17% reduction in depression symptoms would likely be felt as significant by someone suffering, but it’s also possible that it could come from participating in any kind of meaningful psychological change.

article continues after advertisement

On the other hand, the results do fit the broader scientific picture of awe. Generally speaking, two decades of research point to how awe increases well-being through a variety of pathways, including decreased sympathetic nervous system activity and body inflammation, stronger social connections, and a sense of being connected with something larger than oneself.

So what should we do with these findings?

The most cautious answer is that we need more research to know more. One RCT is interesting, but science advances through replication, and the more we find the same patterns of results, the more we can trust them. Future studies will need to determine whether awe interventions outperform other psychological interventions and whether the benefits persist over time.

Source: Vitaly Gariev | Unsplash

At the same time, these findings arrive at a moment when many across the world are trying what are sometimes called "social prescriptions." In addition to medications and traditional therapies, practitioners in some countries now prescribe activities such as spending time in nature, engaging with music and the arts, using spiritual practices, and the like. Although these activities differ in important ways, many of them share something in common: They create opportunities for awe.

It may be premature to prescribe awe by itself as a mental health treatment. But this first randomized controlled trial suggests that the simple practice of paying closer attention to what amazes us may have measurable benefits for psychological well-being.

And if future research confirms these findings, we may discover that one pathway to better mental health begins not with extraordinary experiences, but with learning to notice the extraordinary dimensions of ordinary life.

item.title: When Adult Siblings Don't Get Along
item.description:
Family Dynamics

When Adult Siblings Don't Get Along

Once siblings are on their own, their differences can take their toll.

Posted June 17, 2026

Key points
  • Adult siblings can become estranged. Common causes are different personalities and lack of common interests.
  • Old resentments can also fuel the distance. Sometimes as children age, opportunities open up to reconcile.
  • Parents can assist by helping the children understand why they parented the way they did.
Source: MabeAmber/pixabay

Both Jared and Maggie would agree they were never close growing up. They rarely played together; they had those typical arguments when one crossed the imaginary line down the middle of the car's backseat on long trips, or over who ate all the ice cream. But then, the parents could quell the explosions, or simply pick one up and put them in their room.

Now, as adults, Jared and Maggie obviously no longer fight over the back seat, largely because they are rarely in the same place at the same time. They have little contact, and when they do, it is usually a text about what the other is getting mom or dad for Christmas or birthdays.

Unfortunately, such estrangements are not uncommon. Here are a few of the common sources:

They simply have different personalities

Studies on birth order always talk about how it affects child-rearing and personality: the oldest is a conservative leader, the second is the rebel, the middle child gets lost, and the baby gets babied, all a result of timing and siblings bouncing off each other for parental attention.

They don’t have common interests

While many siblings still find ways to connect as adults, some never do. Parents no longer pressure them into family activities, and, as adults, the siblings have simply moved on to different interests as they become their own persons.

Longstanding resentments rear up

Maggie may walk away from her childhood feeling that older Jared was always the favored child, while Jared may feel resentful that the parents let Maggie, his little sister, get away with things he never could. Both may be true or merely perceptions, but they are sources of hurt that carry over, creating distance.

The underlying dynamic is that, yes, the children were probably treated differently. When Jared was born, the parents were younger, less experienced in parenting, likely had less money, and were both struggling in their early adulthood. By the time Maggie came along, they were more experienced and may have had more money, but they were also more involved in their careers or getting burned out. The bottom line is that, for reasons beyond their control, siblings were often essentially raised by different parents.

article continues after advertisement

What happens next?

Jared and Maggie may continue their distant relationship forever. Or they may reverse course at some point: A family event, such as the death of a grandparent or parent, may bring them together, breaking the longstanding wall of silence. Or, as they get older, their values, needs, and priorities change; they realize they miss the support and connection of family and the sibling relationship.

Closing the gap

Resentments and silence do indeed create a wall. The relationship becomes a staring contest, with each waiting for the other to make a move or a gesture. If it doesn’t come, it only reinforces their stories that the other doesn’t care.

If one or both want to close the gap, the way out is to do it—to take the initiative by reaching out, going beyond two-sentence texts, offering the olive branch, setting aside past resentments, or seeking help through therapy.

If the invitation is accepted, they need to deliberately make time to talk about the past, the present, and the future. If they are stuck in the past and have no new memories to replace them, the past lingers.

The role of parents

I’ve met many parents who come to see me because they are pained by the state of their children's relationships. It is not what they hoped for. They feel guilty or regretful and don’t know how to help close the gap.

article continues after advertisement

What they can do is encourage the siblings to make contact without being pushy. They can help repair the past by acknowledging their role—that yes, they may have treated one differently—and, in a non-defensive way, try to help the individual children understand why they did what they did. They need to apologize for hurting feelings or for not being sensitive enough. The aim is to shift the children’s individual stories toward a more complex picture of the past. If they can do that, they’ve done what they could and need to accept that, as adults, their children will need to work out their own feelings and relationships.

There is no magic bullet here. Relationships heal by changing behaviors that, in turn, change stories and close wounds.

item.title: Why FIFA Feels Bigger Than Football
item.description:
Sport and Competition

Why FIFA Feels Bigger Than Football

What a global tournament reveals about our shared need to matter.

Posted June 17, 2026

Key points
  • Fans become part of a “we,” turning games into shared experiences.
  • Joy feels bigger and heartbreak more bearable when experienced together.
  • Belonging and connection can lead to collective mattering.
  • Beyond sports, communities and causes help us matter together.

I have been enjoying watching some of the FIFA World Cup matches this summer from Vancouver, one of the tournament's host cities. I have not made it to a match in person, but I have found myself just as fascinated by what is happening around the matches. Families crowd around televisions. A restaurant down the street fills with jerseys and flags. Friends text each other to organize watch parties, and strangers who have never met end up trading smiles after a spectacular goal. Entire communities seem to share the anticipation before kickoff and the heartbreak or elation that follows.

Watching this collective enjoyment unfold, I began to wonder whether what draws us to events like the World Cup is about more than sport.

Perhaps it is about our need to matter together.

Research on sports fandom suggests that people derive part of their identity from the groups to which they belong. Fans do not simply watch games; they become part of something larger. Victories become "our victories," and losses become "our disappointments." Researchers have even described an "enlarged sense of we-ness" that develops through shared group membership.

But identity alone is not enough.

Sports are emotional experiences, and those emotions are rarely felt in isolation. Joy and hope, disappointment and relief, are social experiences as much as private ones. Anyone who has held their breath during a penalty shootout or leaped off the couch after a dramatic goal knows the feeling. Even those of us watching from our living rooms know that millions of others around the world are feeling it too, at the very same moment.

Perhaps this is why sports can stir emotions unlike almost anything else. Joy feels bigger when it is shared, and heartbreak feels more bearable when we carry it together. In a fragmented world, these moments remind us that we are part of something beyond ourselves.

How the World Cup Creates Collective Mattering

Three things seem to work together here, and they build toward a fourth.

  • Shared identity. We become part of a "we." Whether it is our national team or simply the city hosting the match, we feel connected to something larger than ourselves.
  • Collective emotions. We celebrate together, and when it goes wrong, we grieve together. The highs and lows of the tournament are experienced not only individually but collectively.
  • Belonging and connection. Families gather, and neighborhoods that are usually quiet come alive with strangers talking to one another. Shared experiences strengthen our sense of belonging and remind us we are not alone.
  • Collective mattering. Together, these build toward something larger — the sense of being valued by, and contributing to, a whole that none of us could create alone. It is what my mentor, the psychologist Dr. Isaac Prilleltensky, called "mattering," experienced collectively.
article continues after advertisement

Everyone adds something, the players and volunteers, yes, but also the host city and the families gathered at home. Whether in the stadium or on a couch across town, people from very different backgrounds come together around the same moment.

In doing so, we are not merely spectators. We are participants in a shared experience.

Beyond the Stadium

The lesson extends far beyond sport. We see the same process in faith communities and in the cultural festivals that fill a city's summer calendar. A shared identity gives rise to shared emotion, and that shared emotion deepens belonging — which is where mattering together begins.

Perhaps this is one reason volunteering or showing up for a cause we believe in so often leaves people feeling fulfilled. We are not only chasing personal happiness. We are seeking experiences that let us matter together.

In an age when loneliness and polarization are increasingly common, perhaps we should pay closer attention to the experiences that bring us together.

Because beneath the goals and the rivalries lies something profoundly human.

We all want to feel valued, and we all want to feel that we add something worth adding.

And sometimes, as millions of people around the world gather around a single game, we are reminded that some of life's greatest moments are not the ones in which we matter alone, but the ones in which we discover that we matter together.

item.title: How Well Can You Spot Happy and Unhappy Strangers?
item.description:
Social Life

How Well Can You Spot Happy and Unhappy Strangers?

Strangers are really good at detecting your mental state in under a minute.

Posted June 17, 2026

Key points
  • Strangers beat chance at reading a person's life satisfaction and positive emotions after a 60-second video.
  • They were no better than chance at reading negative emotions.
  • The cues influencing accurate guesses are voice volume and physical attractiveness.
  • Want to know how someone's really doing? You have to talk to them.

This post is about science that deserves our attention. For example, there is a paper called "Do We Know How Happy Strangers Are? Accuracy in Well-Being Judgments at Zero Acquaintance." It has been referenced fewer than 10 times.

The setup is simple: Adults filled out measures of life satisfaction, frequency of positive emotions, and frequency of negative emotions. Each of them was then videotaped for roughly 60 seconds while introducing themselves and talking freely, the way you would if you were seated next to a stranger at the start of a long night and someone asked, What's the worst hostel story you've got? Four research assistants who never met these people watched the videos and rated each person's well-being using the same measures—excellent use of informant reports and observation methods, by the way. The question: Could strangers, after a one-minute introduction, tell which of these 200 people were doing well?

These Findings Are Not-Obvious

Strangers were significantly better than chance at reading life satisfaction and significantly better than chance at reading positive emotions. But they were terrible at reading negative emotions. That third finding is why this study deserves a big audience, before everyone runs off to babble with Uber drivers.

When the authors looked at which cues were driving the accurate judgments, two mechanisms popped out.

Strangers read people through voice volume and physical attractiveness. Kind of a wacky one-two combo. The volume at which a stranger speaks is being treated as a proxy for how satisfied they are with their entire life. So is whether you find them attractive. These are two cues that have nothing directly to do with the inner experience of the person being judged. You are not an FBI agent assessing the danger of a guy in an airport with shaky hands, eyes darting left to right. You are locked onto decibel levels and a jawline. It reminds me of the lousy proxies people lean on when they choose romantic partners, such as whether they return the shopping cart or not. Dating as a psychologist means enjoying people's pet theories about what makes a good person and a suitable partner, and far more interesting, the tests they use to sort who falls into which category.

The reason negative emotions were unreadable starts to make sense once you see how silly and intuitive this approach to mind reading really is. Guilt does not alter your voice by much. Envy does not influence your hip-to-waist ratio or your bone structure. The slow, exhausting forms of unhappiness that occupy whole years of a person's life sit behind the eyes and do not broadcast through the behavioral cues that thin-slice judgments rely on.

A psychiatrist with a 15-minute intake is running a slightly longer version of the one-minute thin-slice judgment, and the patient who walks in mumbling and average-looking is sending questionable signals at best, which means the doctor has little to write down except a prescription. A jury sees a defendant who is boisterous and clean-shaven and decides he looks like a man worthy of a fine future. The dentist asks how you're doing while her hands are in your mouth, registers that you sound fine, and goes home unaware that her last patient of the day was three weeks out from contemplating suicide. We have built large parts of our social infrastructure around the kind of brief, in-person encounter where the cues that get through carry the least predictive value for what we are actually trying to learn about somebody. The clinical interview, the bail hearing, the teeth cleaning, offer weaker windows than assumed.

article continues after advertisement

People decline social invitations because they predict the experience will be too painful for them and for everyone else. When they do show up, they assume the friend across the table is doing about as well as they appear, which means a private struggle reads as fine. That is what produces the tragic false negatives.

When you start experimenting with your energy ledger, the performance tax, and the diminishing-returns argument for socializing, all of it rests on the assumption that you already know what's going on with the humans you'd skip strolls with. The science discussed here is a demonstration that you suck at this more than you think.

The Fix

Nicholas Epley's lab has shown for years that conversation is the single most reliably underestimated activity in social life. Run the experiment and you find, almost every time, that conversations turn out longer, warmer, and more meaningful than people expected. This study sharpens the edge, because it tells you that half of the well-being picture stays invisible after a thin-slice observation, even when you're convinced you're socially astute. Talking is how you gather the data that thin slices systematically hide.

A few weeks ago I went to a $5 Friday comedy show by myself, sat down with an old-fashioned, and noticed the venue was playing "The Becoming" on the loudspeaker before the lights went down. This is not a popular track but it's one of my favorites, so I was entranced. Ecstatic. Open to whatever the universe might bring, ready to hand over my last Italian rainbow cookie as an offering.

A guy a couple of seats over was alone too, waiting on his partner to come back with drinks, and he had the kind of slumped, glassy expression I would have read as miserable if I'd been running the Choi-Diener-Oishi mental arithmetic. I said something, sort of in his direction but not quite to him, about how many memories this song was dragging up. It was a comment a person could ignore. Instead he started telling me about the first time he heard the album, what he was doing, who he was with. We talked through the whole pre-show, and when his partner came back she joked that we should sit on each other's laps for the rest of the night. If I'd diagnosed him from across the room and trusted my brain, I'd have walked out thinking I spent the evening near human slop, when what I did was sit one Nine Inch Nails song away from somebody about to become my friend.

item.title: What Do Teenagers Think About Misophonia on Social Media?
item.description:
Misophonia

What Do Teenagers Think About Misophonia on Social Media?

Learn from the perspectives of two teenage misophonia advocates.

Posted June 17, 2026

Key points
  • Teenage activists have important views about misophonia representation on social media.
  • They are concerned with social media that characterizes misophonia as only related to anger.
  • They are also concerned about professionals diagnosing misophonia haphazardly via social media.
  • They want accurate representation on social media so that the community can come together.

I have found myself dissatisfied, and even upset, about the way misophonia is portrayed on social media. But who am I to judge, really? I am but one person with one opinion. I was born in the 1960’s, and I didn’t grow up with social media. I grew up during a time when you only had one remote to work the television, and I admit I long for the simplicity of that time. I do not pretend to dismiss the impact social media has across many aspects of our lives, and in my gut, I know that misophonia’s story is being written on social media. I thought, who better to talk to about this than two teenagers with misophonia, both of whom are also advocates: seventeen-year-old Sophie Y of the advocacy group TEAMS (Teens for Education and Advocacy on Misophphonia and seventeen-year-old Kelly M, who led the development of the teen resource page for SoQuiet.

Concerns About Anger and Rage Stereotypes in Misophonia Representation

My first concern about the representation of misophonia on social media has to do with the emphasis on anger and rage. I know that anger is certainly one emotion that a triggered person experiences, but there are many more. I’ve often feared that the public will think of those with misophonia as violent, which is untrue. The following are quotes from Kelly and Sophie addressing this matter in our conversation:

Kelly: I don’t love how it is typically portrayed in social media. I’ve seen so many POV [Point of View] style videos where it's someone acting like they have misophonia and acting triggered by certain sounds, and it always comes off as quite tone deaf. Sure, it introduces more people to the word and the disorder, but anger and discomfort don’t even scratch the surface of what this disorder truly is.

Sophie: I think most of the time, expressing those emotions from people with misophonia is a way to try to connect with other people who feel those adverse emotions. But to bystanders who might not have misophonia or don't understand it, I think misophonia could be misinterpreted as overly aggressive and create this negative stigma around people with misophonia… I would even go as far to say that people with misophonia are actually quite shy and they would rather not be explosive to others. I think that people who experience a lot of frustration and rage with it, rather than turning it outwards, a lot of the time they turn it inwards.

Besides being impressed with the clarity of these answers, I was relieved to know that this wasn’t just my observation and is certainly something that we as a community need to be wary about, and perhaps even try to change.

Issues With Diagnosis and Oversimplification on Social Media

Kelly pointed out another issue that I had not thought about: people are being diagnosed by social media therapists as having misophonia.

article continues after advertisement

Kelly: The other main type of videos I’ve seen are people, doctors, therapists, or other medical professionals saying, “Do you hate the sound of chewing? You may have misophonia.” It often comes off as a way to gain views by exploiting people who may suffer from misophonia but don’t have the name for it yet. It also seems like a cheap way to diagnose someone in the middle of a scroll on social media. It seems like a “hey, so… you hate chewing sounds, this is what’s wrong with you.”

That’s a minefield I am staying away from during this post, but please know Kelly's words are not lost on me. I have always hoped for more ethical behavior amongst those in the medical/mental health field regarding the claims that professionals make in terms of “curing” misophonia. I had not thought about what it must feel like for a teenager to be haphazardly and perhaps inaccurately diagnosed via TikTok or Instagram, etc. I wrote about this ten years ago in my blog, and I thought that since we have misophonia measures now, this problem would be attenuating. Obviously not.

Sophie also brought up a very astute observation during our conversation:

Sophie: And I also wanted to add that I think it's hard to understand the complications with misophonia and the little things, because you know, social media is very geared to summarizing things... And I think a lot of things are lost in translation, and I think that's one thing creators can kind of end up falling into a little with that.

That was an eye-opener for me as well, but now it seems so obvious when I mull over it! Social media is a summarizing vehicle. Misophonia is a very complex disorder. The same is true of other conditions. Yet, misophonia is relatively new, and the background knowledge necessary to begin to understand misophonia is nascent and is still not widely available. Accurate summaries can be misleading. Imprecise summaries easily approach mistruth.

How Teens With Misophonia Want Representation to Improve

Finally, I asked both Kelly and Sophie how they each wanted to see misophonia represented on social media. I will end this post with their answers because they most certainly speak for themselves.

Sophie: I think as time goes on, it will improve, but I feel that because misophonia is such an underrepresented community still in social media, people are just trying to get the word out there, which is both helping our community, but can also bring a few downsides. But yeah, still good to bring awareness though.

article continues after advertisement

Kelly: I want to see more people talking about misophonia in a positive and accurate way! Yes, absolutely, it is a struggle that so many of us deal with each and every day, but it shouldn’t be taboo to discuss or something that people don’t want to hear about. It is a community of so many people that support one another and come together to lift each other up. We need allies more than ever. Social media is something that millions and millions of people use each day to learn, discover, and create. When we use social media to accurately represent us, it has the ability to work wonders for public understanding of who we are.
